laws.title: New Zealand Constitution Act 1986
laws.subtitle: Unwritten constitution and parliamentary sovereignty
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand has no single written constitution — its constitutional arrangements derive from multiple sources including the Constitution Act 1986, the Electoral Act 1993, the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act 1990, the Treaty of Waitangi, and constitutional conventions. Parliamentary sovereignty is the foundational principle. New Zealand has a unicameral parliament (abolished Senate 1950). The Governor-General represents King Charles III as head of state.
laws.penalty: Constitutional violations adjudicated by courts; no direct criminal penalties
exceptions: NZBORA rights can be limited by demonstrably justified laws
Prerogative powers of Crown reserved for emergencies

quiz.q: What type of legislature does New Zealand have (how many chambers)?
quiz.explanation: New Zealand has a unicameral parliament with only the House of Representatives, having abolished its Legislative Council (upper house/Senate) in 1950, making it one of the few Westminster-style unicameral democracies.

laws.title: Treaty of Waitangi 1840
laws.subtitle: Māori rights and Crown obligations
laws.fullDescription: The Treaty of Waitangi, signed in 1840 between the British Crown and Māori chiefs, is New Zealand's founding constitutional document. The Māori version (te Tiriti) and English version have significant textual differences around sovereignty (rangatiratanga/kawanatanga). The Waitangi Tribunal (established 1975) hears Māori grievances. Treaty principles — partnership, protection, and participation — inform much NZ legislation.
laws.penalty: Treaty violations addressed through Waitangi Tribunal; Crown settlements compensate historical grievances
exceptions: Treaty doesn't grant veto power over legislation
Treaty settlements are full and final

quiz.q: In what year was the Waitangi Tribunal established to hear Māori grievances?
quiz.explanation: The Waitangi Tribunal was established in 1975 by the Treaty of Waitangi Act, initially with limited powers to investigate contemporary Treaty breaches, later (1985) given power to investigate historical claims back to 1840.

laws.title: Mixed Member Proportional (MMP) Voting
laws.subtitle: Electoral system and proportional representation
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand adopted the Mixed Member Proportional (MMP) system in 1996 following a referendum, replacing First Past the Post. MMP gives voters two votes — one for an electorate MP and one for a party. Parties that win at least 5% of the party vote or one electorate seat enter parliament proportionally. The 2023 election brought National, ACT, and NZ First into government. Māori electorate seats are a feature of the system.
laws.penalty: Electoral offenses: fines; illegal campaign spending: serious criminal penalties
exceptions: Parties below 5% threshold can still enter if they win an electorate
Special votes (overseas, late enrollers) counted after election night

quiz.q: What minimum party vote percentage does a party need to enter NZ parliament under MMP?
quiz.explanation: Under New Zealand's MMP system, a party needs to win at least 5% of the party vote (or win at least one electorate seat) to enter parliament and receive proportional representation based on their party vote share.

laws.title: Crimes Act 1961 and Criminal Justice
laws.subtitle: Core criminal law and sentencing
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand's Crimes Act 1961 is the primary criminal statute. New Zealand has a relatively low crime rate compared to peers but significant disparities — Māori make up 16% of the population but over 50% of the prison population. The Sentencing Act 2002 governs penalties. The 2021-2022 policy of reducing imprisonment ('Let's Get Wellington Moving') under Labour was reversed by National in 2023 with tougher sentencing policies.
laws.penalty: Murder: life imprisonment (minimum 17 years non-parole); serious assault: up to 14 years
exceptions: Youth offenders (under 17) handled in Family Court
Restorative justice conferences available for some offenses

quiz.q: Māori make up approximately what percentage of New Zealand's prison population despite being 16% of the total population?
quiz.explanation: Despite comprising approximately 16% of New Zealand's total population, Māori make up over 50% of the prison population, a stark disparity reflecting historical disadvantage, socioeconomic inequality, and systemic issues in the justice system.

laws.title: Marriage (Definition of Marriage) Amendment Act 2013
laws.subtitle: Marriage equality in New Zealand
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand legalized same-sex marriage in April 2013 under the Marriage (Definition of Marriage) Amendment Act, becoming the 13th country in the world and first in the Asia-Pacific to do so. The vote was 77-44 in parliament. The public gallery broke into a spontaneous rendition of a Māori love song ('Pokarekare Ana') after the vote. New Zealand had previously provided civil unions since 2005.
laws.penalty: Discrimination against same-sex couples in marriage services: Human Rights Commission proceedings
exceptions: Religious celebrants can opt out of solemnizing same-sex marriages
Religious organizations retain some employment exemptions

quiz.q: What spontaneous event occurred in the New Zealand parliament gallery after the marriage equality vote?
options: The public sang a Māori love song
A standing ovation that lasted 10 minutes
Protesters threw flowers into the chamber
quiz.explanation: After the 77-44 vote to legalize same-sex marriage, the public gallery in New Zealand's parliament spontaneously broke into song, singing 'Pokarekare Ana' (a traditional Māori love song), in a memorable moment of national celebration.

laws.title: Resource Management Act 1991 / RMA Reform
laws.subtitle: Planning law and environmental management
laws.fullDescription: The Resource Management Act 1991 (RMA) is New Zealand's primary environmental planning statute, governing land use, coastal management, and resource consent. Widely criticized for creating slow, expensive consent processes that impede housing construction, the RMA has been the subject of repeated reform attempts. The Fast-track Approvals Act 2024 (National-led government) created an alternative streamlined pathway for significant projects.
laws.penalty: RMA violations: fines up to NZ$600,000; enforcement orders; abatement notices
exceptions: Permitted activities need no resource consent
National Policy Statements can override local plans
laws.sourceLabel: Ministry for the Environment NZ RMA

quiz.q: What is New Zealand's primary environmental planning statute?
quiz.explanation: The Resource Management Act 1991 (RMA) is New Zealand's primary environmental planning law, governing land use, coastal management, water management, and the resource consent process for significant developments.

laws.title: New Zealand Health System Reform 2022
laws.subtitle: Health NZ / Te Whatu Ora and Māori Health Authority
laws.fullDescription: In 2022, New Zealand abolished its 20 District Health Boards and replaced them with Health New Zealand (Te Whatu Ora) — a single national health authority — and the Māori Health Authority (Te Aka Whai Ora). The Māori Health Authority was disestablished by the incoming National government in 2023 in a controversial move. New Zealand has universal healthcare funded by general taxation, with primary care supplemented by patient co-payments.
laws.penalty: Healthcare fraud: criminal prosecution; patient safety violations: regulatory sanctions
exceptions: ACC (accident compensation) covers treatment for accidental injuries regardless of fault
Private health insurance voluntary but widely used for elective surgery
laws.sourceLabel: Health New Zealand Te Whatu Ora

quiz.q: What was the name of the Māori-specific health body established in 2022 and then disestablished in 2023?
options: Te Aka Whai Ora (Māori Health Authority)
quiz.explanation: Te Aka Whai Ora (the Māori Health Authority) was established in 2022 to specifically address Māori health outcomes, but was disestablished by the incoming National-led government in 2023, a move Māori groups strongly opposed.

laws.title: Emissions Trading Scheme / Agricultural Emissions
laws.subtitle: Farming and climate policy
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand's Emissions Trading Scheme (NZ ETS) is the primary carbon pricing mechanism. Uniquely globally, New Zealand has been debating whether to include agricultural emissions (from livestock belching methane) in the ETS — agriculture accounts for nearly 50% of NZ's emissions. The He Waka Eke Noa farm-level pricing system was proposed as an alternative. The National government in 2023 stepped back from mandatory agricultural emissions pricing.
laws.penalty: ETS non-compliance: significant financial penalties and liability for excess emissions
exceptions: Agricultural free allocation of units reduces cost
Some forestry activities generate NZUs (New Zealand Units)

quiz.q: Approximately what percentage of New Zealand's greenhouse gas emissions come from agriculture?
quiz.explanation: Agriculture accounts for nearly 50% of New Zealand's greenhouse gas emissions (primarily methane from livestock and nitrous oxide from fertilizers), making it a uniquely challenging sector in NZ's climate policy compared to most other developed countries.

laws.title: Arms (Prohibited Firearms) Amendment Act 2019
laws.subtitle: Post-Christchurch mosque attack gun reform
laws.fullDescription: Following the Christchurch mosque terrorist attacks (51 killed, 40 wounded) on 15 March 2019, Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern's government passed the Arms (Prohibited Firearms, Magazines, and Parts) Amendment Act within 26 days, banning military-style semi-automatic weapons. The buyback collected around 60,000 firearms. A second arms reform addressed online extremism and the Christchurch Call initiative with France sought to prevent terrorist content online.
laws.penalty: Possession of prohibited firearms: up to 5 years imprisonment
exceptions: Licensed collectors with specific permits for historical weapons
Police and military retain use of prohibited firearms

quiz.q: How quickly did New Zealand pass firearms reform legislation after the Christchurch attacks?
quiz.explanation: New Zealand passed the Arms (Prohibited Firearms) Amendment Act within just 26 days of the Christchurch mosque attacks on 15 March 2019, with near-unanimous parliamentary support, banning military-style semi-automatic weapons.

laws.title: Employment Relations Act 2000
laws.subtitle: Worker rights and collective bargaining
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand's Employment Relations Act 2000 provides for individual employment agreements, good faith obligations, and collective bargaining. The minimum wage is regularly reviewed (NZ$22.70/hour from April 2024). NZ has introduced sick leave improvements (10 days from 2021) and bereavement leave extensions. The "Fair Pay Agreements" system — sector-wide collective agreements — was introduced by Labour and repealed by National in 2023.
laws.penalty: Employment law violations: mediation; Employment Relations Authority; Employment Court awards
exceptions: Small employers have modified redundancy provisions
Trial periods for new employees (90 days) reinstated by National government

quiz.q: What sector-wide collective bargaining system did New Zealand's Labour government introduce (and National later repeal)?
quiz.explanation: The Fair Pay Agreements system, introduced by the Labour government in 2022, allowed workers to initiate sector-wide collective bargaining covering entire industries. The incoming National government repealed it in 2023.

laws.title: Privacy Act 2020 / Notifiable Breaches
laws.subtitle: Privacy law reform and data protection
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand's Privacy Act 2020 replaced the 1993 Act, introducing mandatory notification of privacy breaches that cause or are likely to cause serious harm (notifiable privacy breaches). The Privacy Commissioner can investigate complaints and issue compliance notices. New Zealand has been active in the development of AI ethics guidelines. The GCSB (Government Communications Security Bureau) monitors cybersecurity threats.
laws.penalty: Fines up to NZ$10,000 for privacy breaches (individual) or NZ$50,000 for organisations (under review for increase)
exceptions: Law enforcement activities exempted from some privacy principles
Journalism and research exemptions apply

quiz.q: What new requirement did New Zealand's Privacy Act 2020 introduce compared to the 1993 Act?
options: Mandatory notification of privacy breaches causing serious harm
quiz.explanation: New Zealand's Privacy Act 2020 introduced mandatory notifiable privacy breach reporting — organizations must notify the Privacy Commissioner and affected individuals of privacy breaches that cause or could cause serious harm.

laws.title: Income Tax Act 2007 / GST
laws.subtitle: Tax system and fiscal policy
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand has a relatively simple tax system — a 15% Goods and Services Tax (GST) applying broadly (including food, unlike Australia), and income tax rates up to 39% (top rate introduced 2021 for income over NZ$180,000). There is no capital gains tax on most assets (ongoing political debate). Inland Revenue (Te Tari Taake) administers tax. New Zealand has a high-trust, self-assessment approach.
laws.penalty: Tax evasion: up to 5 years imprisonment; civil penalties up to 150% of shortfall
exceptions: Bright-line test treats property sold within 10 years as taxable
GST registered businesses can claim input tax credits

quiz.q: What is New Zealand's GST (Goods and Services Tax) rate?
quiz.explanation: New Zealand's GST rate is 15%, applying broadly to most goods and services including food — unlike Australia where many food items are GST-exempt. GST was introduced in 1986 and raised to 15% in 2010.

laws.title: Housing Affordability Crisis / Housing First
laws.subtitle: Housing crisis and homelessness policy
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand's housing crisis is among the developed world's most severe — house prices-to-income ratios in Auckland and Wellington are among the highest globally. The Labour government introduced the Kāinga Ora (Homes and Communities) social housing program and attempted to restrict overseas house purchases. The National government's housing policy focuses on planning deregulation and intensification. Homelessness, including rough sleeping and emergency housing motels, increased significantly during 2020-2023.
laws.penalty: Illegal evictions: Tenancy Tribunal orders; health and safety violations in rental properties: fines
exceptions: Community housing providers have special funding arrangements
Emergency housing grants for acute need

quiz.q: Which New Zealand city has among the world's worst house price-to-income ratios?
quiz.explanation: Auckland has one of the world's worst housing affordability crises, with house price-to-income ratios that rival or exceed London, Sydney, and Hong Kong, reflecting extreme supply constraints in a geographically constrained city.

laws.title: Immigration Act 2009 / Pacific Access Category
laws.subtitle: Migration and Pacific Island connections
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand's Immigration Act 2009 governs migration. New Zealand has special arrangements for Pacific Islanders — Samoa Agreement (1970), Tuvalu and Kiribati access categories, and the Pacific Access Category ballot for Fiji, Tonga, and others. Free movement exists for NZ and Australian citizens between the two countries. The Recognised Seasonal Employer (RSE) scheme allows Pacific Island workers into horticulture.
laws.penalty: Overstaying visa: deportation; working without authorization: criminal penalties
exceptions: Australian citizens have automatic right to live and work in NZ
Pacific Access Category ballot winners gain residence

quiz.q: What allows New Zealand and Australian citizens to move freely between the two countries?
quiz.explanation: The Trans-Tasman Travel Arrangement (not a formal treaty but a long-standing bilateral policy) allows New Zealand and Australian citizens to live and work in each other's country without requiring a visa, reflecting the close relationship between the two nations.

laws.title: Marine and Coastal Area Act 2011
laws.subtitle: Foreshore and seabed / Māori customary rights
laws.fullDescription: The Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011 replaced the controversial Foreshore and Seabed Act 2004, which had extinguished Māori customary title to coastal areas and triggered the formation of the Māori Party. The 2011 Act allows Māori groups to apply for customary marine title and protected customary rights. Hundreds of applications have been filed; courts have been processing claims over more than a decade.
laws.penalty: Breaching customary marine title orders: civil and regulatory consequences
exceptions: Public rights of access to coastal marine area preserved
Existing resource consents for coastal activities continue

quiz.q: What Māori political party was formed largely as a response to the controversial Foreshore and Seabed Act 2004?
quiz.explanation: The Māori Party (Te Pāti Māori) was formed in 2004 largely in response to the Labour government's Foreshore and Seabed Act, which was seen by Māori as extinguishing their customary title to coastal areas.

laws.title: Terrorism Suppression Act 2002 / Christchurch Call
laws.subtitle: Counter-terrorism and online extremism
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand's Terrorism Suppression Act 2002 defines and criminalizes terrorist acts. The Christchurch mosque attacks (2019) by a white nationalist terrorist exposed gaps in pre-attack intelligence sharing and online radicalization. The Royal Commission of Inquiry (He Whenua Taurikura) recommended significant intelligence reforms. The Christchurch Call — a joint initiative by NZ PM Ardern and French President Macron — commits governments and tech companies to eliminate terrorist and extremist content online.
laws.penalty: Terrorism offenses: up to life imprisonment; financing terrorism: up to 14 years
exceptions: Legitimate journalism and research involving terrorist content
Intelligence operations targeting terrorism

quiz.q: Who co-initiated the Christchurch Call alongside NZ PM Jacinda Ardern?
quiz.explanation: The Christchurch Call was jointly initiated by NZ Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern and French President Emmanuel Macron in May 2019, committing governments and tech companies to eliminate terrorist and violent extremist content online.

laws.title: Climate Change Response Act / Zero Carbon
laws.subtitle: Zero Carbon Act and emissions budgets
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand's Climate Change Response (Zero Carbon) Amendment Act 2019 set targets of net-zero long-lived greenhouse gases by 2050, with biogenic methane from agriculture to be reduced 24-47% by 2050. An independent Climate Change Commission (He Pou a Rangi) advises on emissions budgets. NZ has legally binding carbon budgets. Floods and cyclone Gabrielle (2023) — NZ's most expensive natural disaster — heightened climate urgency.
laws.penalty: Government must comply with budgets; no direct criminal penalties on individuals
exceptions: Agricultural methane has separate targets from CO2 and other long-lived gases
Offshore aviation and shipping not counted in NZ's targets

quiz.q: By what year does NZ's Zero Carbon Act require net-zero long-lived greenhouse gases?
quiz.explanation: New Zealand's Climate Change Response (Zero Carbon) Amendment Act 2019 requires net-zero long-lived greenhouse gases (CO2, N2O, etc.) by 2050, with separate targets for biogenic methane from agriculture.

laws.title: Domestic Violence Act 2018 / Safety Leave
laws.subtitle: Family violence law and workplace protections
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand's Family Violence Act 2018 consolidated domestic violence legislation, defining 'family violence' broadly to include psychological abuse, financial abuse, and coercive control. The Domestic Violence—Victims' Protection Act 2018 gives domestic violence victims up to 10 days of paid safety leave from work to address their situation — a world-first employment provision. New Zealand has a high rate of family violence.
laws.penalty: Domestic violence offenses: up to 3 years; breaching protection orders: up to 3 years
exceptions: Restorative justice processes available for suitable cases
Safety Planning included in intervention framework

quiz.q: What world-first employment provision did New Zealand introduce for domestic violence victims?
options: Free legal aid for court proceedings
Up to 10 days paid safety leave from work
quiz.explanation: New Zealand was the first country in the world to legislate paid 'safety leave' for domestic violence victims — up to 10 days annually — under the Domestic Violence—Victims' Protection Act 2018.

laws.title: Sentencing Act 2002 / Three Strikes
laws.subtitle: Criminal sentencing and law and order debate
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand's Sentencing Act 2002 governs criminal penalties. The Three Strikes Legislation (2010), which imposed life imprisonment for a third serious violent offense, was repealed by Labour in 2022 as ineffective and disproportionate. The incoming National government (2023) reinstated three strikes. New Zealand has ongoing debate about its relatively high rate of imprisonment per capita and the effectiveness of rehabilitation versus punitive approaches.
laws.penalty: Violent offenses: varying terms; murder: life imprisonment (up to 17 years non-parole)
exceptions: Youth court handles offenders under 17
Parole for eligible prisoners reduces time served

quiz.q: What happened to New Zealand's 'Three Strikes' legislation between 2010 and 2024?
options: It was passed in 2010 and never changed
It was repealed by Labour in 2022 and reinstated by National in 2023
It was struck down by the Supreme Court
It has been continuously in force since 2010
quiz.explanation: New Zealand's Three Strikes law was passed in 2010 (National government), repealed in 2022 (Labour government) as ineffective and cruel, and then reinstated by the incoming National-led government in 2023 as part of its law and order platform.

laws.title: Companies Act 1993 / Financial Markets Conduct
laws.subtitle: Corporate law and FMA regulation
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand's Companies Act 1993 is the primary corporate law, with the Financial Markets Authority (FMA) as the securities regulator. The Financial Markets Conduct Act 2013 modernized financial services regulation. NZ has been an early adopter of integrated reporting and climate-related financial disclosures — the Financial Sector (Climate-related Disclosures and Other Matters) Amendment Act 2021 requires large financial firms to disclose climate risks.
laws.penalty: Director duty breaches: civil penalties up to NZ$500,000; criminal prosecution for serious breaches
exceptions: Small companies (under 10 shareholders, no public share offer) have reduced obligations
Registered charities have modified governance rules

quiz.q: What historic requirement did NZ's 2021 Financial Sector Amendment Act impose on large financial firms?
quiz.explanation: New Zealand's 2021 Financial Sector (Climate-related Disclosures) Amendment Act was among the world's first to mandate climate-related financial disclosures for large financial institutions, insurers, and listed companies.

laws.title: Misuse of Drugs Act 1975 / Drug Reform
laws.subtitle: Drug policy and 2020 cannabis referendum
laws.fullDescription: The Misuse of Drugs Act 1975 classifies controlled drugs into Classes A, B, and C. The 2020 Cannabis Legalisation and Control Bill referendum was narrowly defeated (53-46 No). New Zealand decriminalized personal drug use in 2019 (police discretion to divert to health services). Methamphetamine (P) is the most significant illicit drug in NZ. A 2024 review of drug policy is examining whether to remove criminal penalties for personal use.
laws.penalty: Class A supply (e.g., heroin, meth): life imprisonment; personal use: police discretion for health referral
exceptions: Medicinal cannabis scheme allows doctor prescription
Drug checking services at festivals legally permitted
laws.sourceLabel: NZ Ministry of Health Drug Policy

quiz.q: What was the result of New Zealand's 2020 cannabis legalization referendum?
quiz.explanation: New Zealand's 2020 cannabis legalization referendum was narrowly defeated by 53.1% No to 46.1% Yes, meaning cannabis remained illegal for recreational use, though the vote was much closer than most polls had predicted.

laws.title: Consumer Guarantees Act 1993 / FDR
laws.subtitle: Consumer rights and financial disputes
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand's Consumer Guarantees Act 1993 implies guarantees that goods must be fit for purpose and services must be provided with reasonable care and skill. The Financial Dispute Resolution scheme provides low-cost resolution of financial services complaints. The Commerce Commission enforces fair trading and competition law. Consumer protection has been strengthened with credit contract reforms and insurance disclosure requirements.
laws.penalty: Breach of consumer guarantees: supplier must repair, replace, or refund; Commerce Commission fines for misleading conduct
exceptions: Goods purchased for business purposes have different rules
Private sales between individuals partially exempt

quiz.q: Under New Zealand's Consumer Guarantees Act, what must suppliers do if goods are not of acceptable quality?
options: Refer the matter to a mediator
quiz.explanation: Under the Consumer Guarantees Act 1993, if goods are not of acceptable quality, suppliers must repair, replace, or provide a refund — the consumer can choose between these remedies in most circumstances.

laws.title: Accident Compensation Act 2001 / ACC
laws.subtitle: No-fault accident compensation scheme
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand's Accident Compensation Corporation (ACC) provides no-fault insurance for personal injuries from accidents, regardless of how the accident occurred or who was at fault. This means New Zealanders generally cannot sue for personal injury from accidents — the right to sue was abolished in exchange for universal no-fault compensation. ACC covers medical treatment, rehabilitation, and income compensation (80% of pre-injury income). Mental injury from physical injury and criminal acts is covered.
laws.penalty: Providing false information to ACC: criminal offense; employers must pay levies
exceptions: Medical misadventure has separate treatment injury claims
Gradual process injuries (eg. hearing loss) have modified rules

quiz.q: What right did New Zealanders give up in exchange for the ACC no-fault compensation scheme?
options: The right to vote in workplace safety referendums
The right to sue in court for personal injury from accidents
The right to choose their own doctor
The right to unemployment benefits if injured
quiz.explanation: New Zealanders generally cannot sue for personal injury resulting from accidents — the right to sue for accident-related personal injury was abolished when ACC was established, replaced by a universal no-fault compensation scheme.

laws.title: International Students / Education Export
laws.subtitle: International education and immigration pathway
laws.fullDescription: International students are a major export earner for New Zealand, contributing NZ$5 billion+ to the economy pre-COVID. The sector collapsed during COVID-19 border closures. Immigration rules allow international students to work during study and after graduation (graduate visas). New Zealand's Skilled Migrant Category provides a pathway to residence. Exploitation of international students and workers on temporary visas has been a significant concern.
laws.penalty: Exploitation of migrant workers: criminal penalties for employers; civil fines
exceptions: Post-study work visas linked to study duration
Partner working rights included in some student visas

quiz.q: What was the approximate value of New Zealand's international education export industry pre-COVID?
quiz.explanation: International education was worth over NZ$5 billion to New Zealand's economy before COVID-19, making it one of the country's largest services exports, before collapsing when borders closed in 2020.

laws.title: Broadcasting Act 1989 / RNZ and TVNZ
laws.subtitle: Public broadcasting and media reform
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand's broadcasting system includes Radio New Zealand (RNZ, public, no advertising) and TVNZ (public, commercially funded). Labour's plan to merge TVNZ and RNZ into a combined public broadcaster was abandoned after years of planning and NZ$60 million spent. The News Media Assistance Programme (NZ MAP) provides contestable public interest journalism funding. Misinformation, particularly around COVID-19, tested NZ media law.
laws.penalty: Broadcasting Standards Authority can impose fines and order on-air corrections
exceptions: On-demand services have lighter regulatory requirements
Community broadcasters have different funding and obligations

quiz.q: Which planned reform of New Zealand's public broadcasting sector was abandoned after NZ$60 million was spent on planning?
quiz.explanation: Labour's proposal to merge Television New Zealand (TVNZ) and Radio New Zealand (RNZ) into a combined public media entity was abandoned in 2023 after approximately NZ$60 million had been spent on planning and preparation.

laws.title: CPTPP and Trade Agreements
laws.subtitle: NZ trade policy and the Pacific
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand has a comprehensive free trade agreement network. The CPTPP (signed 2018) is the backbone of NZ's Asia-Pacific trade strategy. NZ concluded the UK-NZ FTA (2022) and is part of RCEP. China is NZ's largest trading partner (FTA signed 2008). NZ's primary exports — dairy, meat, wool, seafood, wine — depend heavily on market access. NZ is a strong advocate for agricultural trade liberalization through the Cairns Group at the WTO.
laws.penalty: Trade violations sanctioned through WTO and bilateral dispute mechanisms
exceptions: CPTPP investor-state dispute resolution provisions
Agricultural sensitive product tariff phase-outs

quiz.q: With which major Asian country did New Zealand sign its first FTA in 2008?
quiz.explanation: New Zealand signed a Free Trade Agreement with China in 2008 — the first developed country in the world to do so — marking a significant shift in NZ's trade priorities and deepening its economic relationship with China.

laws.title: Intelligence and Security Act 2017 / Five Eyes
laws.subtitle: GCSB, NZSIS and intelligence law
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand's Intelligence and Security Act 2017 consolidated the law governing the GCSB (signals intelligence) and NZSIS (security intelligence). New Zealand is a member of the Five Eyes intelligence alliance (with the US, UK, Canada, and Australia). Post-Christchurch, intelligence on right-wing extremism has increased. New Zealand is part of AUKUS's Pillar 2 (technology sharing) but not the submarine component. The Inspector-General of Intelligence provides oversight.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized intelligence disclosure: up to 2 years imprisonment
exceptions: Whistleblower protections for lawful disclosures through appropriate channels
Parliamentary committee oversight

quiz.q: What is the intelligence-sharing alliance that New Zealand participates in?
quiz.explanation: New Zealand is a member of the Five Eyes intelligence alliance, which shares signals intelligence and security information between Australia, Canada, New Zealand, the United Kingdom, and the United States.

laws.title: Māori Electoral Option / Seats
laws.subtitle: Māori electorates and dual roll
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand has 7 dedicated Māori electorate seats in parliament, allocated based on the Māori roll population. Māori can choose to enroll on either the general roll or the Māori roll ('Māori Electoral Option'). Under MMP, Māori parties that win electorate seats can bring in additional list MPs. The Māori Party and Te Pāti Māori have represented Māori electoral interests since 2004. ACT proposes abolishing Māori seats.
laws.penalty: Enrollment offenses: fines; voting in wrong electorate: electoral offense
exceptions: Māori can change rolls at each option period (usually every 5 years)
Māori party list MPs don't count against electorate overhang

quiz.q: How many dedicated Māori electorate seats does New Zealand's parliament currently have?
quiz.explanation: New Zealand's parliament currently has 7 dedicated Māori electorate seats, allocated proportionally based on the number of Māori who enroll on the Māori roll rather than the general roll.

laws.title: First country for women's suffrage / Gender equality
laws.subtitle: 1893 suffrage anniversary and gender parity
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand was the first self-governing country in the world to grant women the right to vote, in 1893 — largely through the efforts of Kate Sheppard and the Women's Christian Temperance Union. New Zealand has had three women Prime Ministers (Helen Clark, Jenny Shipley, Jacinda Ardern). However, gender pay gap persists (~9%), and women are underrepresented in corporate leadership. The Pay Equity Act 2020 provides mechanisms for sector-wide pay equity claims.
laws.penalty: Gender pay discrimination: Employment Relations Authority awards
exceptions: Pay equity claims involve sector-wide analysis
Market rates may influence pay regardless of gender
laws.sourceLabel: NZ Ministry for Culture and Heritage Women's Suffrage

quiz.q: In what year did New Zealand become the first self-governing country to grant women the right to vote?
quiz.explanation: New Zealand granted women the right to vote in 1893, making it the first self-governing country in the world to do so, with the Electoral Act signed by Governor Lord Glasgow on 19 September 1893.

laws.title: New Zealand Bill of Rights Act 1990
laws.subtitle: NZBORA and human rights protection
laws.fullDescription: The New Zealand Bill of Rights Act 1990 protects civil and political rights but is not supreme law — Parliament can legislate inconsistently with it. The Attorney-General must report to Parliament on any bill that appears to be inconsistent with NZBORA. Courts can interpret legislation to be consistent with NZBORA 'where possible'. The Supreme Court (established 2004) is the final court of appeal. Calls for a supreme law bill of rights continue in academic and political circles.
laws.penalty: NZBORA violations compensated through civil law; Baigent's case allows damages for rights breaches by government
exceptions: Rights can be limited by 'reasonable limits prescribed by law that can be demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society' (s.5)
National security derogations possible

quiz.q: What must the NZ Attorney-General do if a bill appears inconsistent with the Bill of Rights Act?
options: Report to Parliament about the inconsistency
Refer the bill to the Supreme Court
Seek public referendum on the inconsistent provision
quiz.explanation: Under Section 7 of NZBORA, the Attorney-General must report to Parliament if any bill appears to be inconsistent with the Bill of Rights Act, though Parliament can still pass the bill regardless — it is not automatically blocked.

laws.title: Marine Mammals Protection Act 1978
laws.subtitle: Hectors dolphins and marine conservation
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand's marine environment is globally significant — Hector's and Māui dolphins are the world's smallest and rarest dolphins, found only in NZ waters. The Marine Mammals Protection Act 1978 and Marine Protected Areas policy protect these species. Commercial fishing entanglement is the primary threat. NZ's 1.7 million km2 EEZ is one of the world's largest but fisheries management has been controversial.
laws.penalty: Harming or disturbing marine mammals: up to NZ$250,000 fines; commercial fishing in restricted areas: license cancellation
exceptions: Traditional Māori fishing rights recognized
Research activities with permits

quiz.q: What distinguishes Hector's and Māui dolphins, found in NZ waters?
options: They are the largest dolphin species
They are found across the Pacific
They are the world's smallest and rarest dolphins
They are the fastest swimming dolphins
quiz.explanation: Hector's dolphin and its subspecies the Māui dolphin are the world's smallest and rarest dolphins, found only in New Zealand waters. The Māui dolphin is critically endangered with fewer than 100 individuals remaining.

laws.title: Serious Fraud Office Act 1990 / Transparency
laws.subtitle: SFO and anti-corruption
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand's Serious Fraud Office investigates serious and complex financial crime including bribery, money laundering, and securities fraud. New Zealand consistently ranks as one of the world's least corrupt countries (typically top 3 in Transparency International's CPI). The Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Act 2009 has been progressively extended to include lawyers, accountants, and real estate agents.
laws.penalty: Bribery: up to 7 years imprisonment; money laundering: up to 7 years
exceptions: Facilitation payments (common in some jurisdictions) are treated as bribery in NZ
Cooperation with SFO can reduce sentences

quiz.q: How does New Zealand typically rank on Transparency International's Corruption Perceptions Index?
quiz.explanation: New Zealand consistently ranks as one of the world's least corrupt countries, typically in the top 3 on Transparency International's Corruption Perceptions Index alongside Denmark and Finland.

laws.title: Medicinal Cannabis Scheme
laws.subtitle: Medical cannabis and drug reform
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand's Medicinal Cannabis Scheme, established under the Misuse of Drugs Amendment Act 2019, allows licensed cultivation, manufacture, and supply of medicinal cannabis products. Patients with serious medical conditions can access cannabis-based medicines with a prescription. New Zealand failed the 2020 cannabis legalization referendum (recreational use) by a narrow margin. The legal medicinal cannabis market is growing.
laws.penalty: Cultivation or supply of cannabis outside the scheme: up to 14 years imprisonment
exceptions: Licensed producers can legally cultivate and process
Personal possession for medical use with prescription

quiz.q: Under what amendment act was New Zealand's Medicinal Cannabis Scheme established?
quiz.explanation: New Zealand's Medicinal Cannabis Scheme was established under the Misuse of Drugs (Medicinal Cannabis) Amendment Act 2019, creating a licensed framework for the cultivation, manufacture, and supply of medicinal cannabis products.

laws.title: Corrections Act 2004 / Prison Reform
laws.subtitle: Prisons and rehabilitation
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand's Corrections Act 2004 governs the management of prisons and community sentences. NZ has a high imprisonment rate relative to its population, particularly of Māori. The 2019 'Hōkai Rangi' Corrections strategy aimed to reduce Māori imprisonment. Several prison closures and conversions to rehabilitation-focused facilities occurred under Labour. Corrections Department administers electronic monitoring, home detention, and community service.
laws.penalty: Prison sentences determined by Sentencing Act; parole eligibility after minimum served
exceptions: Home detention for lower risk offenders
Youth justice — Family Group Conferences for under-17s

quiz.q: What is the name of New Zealand Corrections' strategy aimed at reducing Māori imprisonment rates?
quiz.explanation: 'Hōkai Rangi' (a Māori phrase meaning 'the path to the sky') is the Corrections Department's strategic framework for reducing Māori imprisonment rates and improving outcomes for Māori offenders and victims.

laws.title: Overseas Investment Act 2005
laws.subtitle: Foreign land purchases and Māori land
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand's Overseas Investment Act 2005 (significantly amended 2018 and 2020) restricts overseas buyers from purchasing sensitive New Zealand land including residential property, farmland, and land near coastlines. The 2018 amendment — targeting overseas house buyers — was a political response to housing affordability concerns and Chinese investment debate. Māori land (Māori freehold land) has special protections preventing sale outside the whanau (family).
laws.penalty: Completing overseas investment without consent: criminal fines; forced disposal orders
exceptions: Australian citizens have modified rules under CER
Certain investments in rural land with conditions allowed

quiz.q: When was the significant amendment that restricted overseas buyers from purchasing NZ residential property?
quiz.explanation: The Overseas Investment Amendment Act 2018 significantly restricted overseas buyers (outside Australia) from purchasing existing New Zealand residential properties, responding to housing affordability concerns and debate about foreign investment in housing.

laws.title: Harmful Digital Communications Act 2015
laws.subtitle: Online bullying and harassment law
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand's Harmful Digital Communications Act 2015 (HDCA) created civil and criminal mechanisms to address online bullying, harassment, and threats. A government-approved agency (NetSafe) provides mediation services. Criminal offenses apply for the most serious digital communications. The act has been used in cases of cyberbullying leading to suicide, sextortion, and online harassment campaigns. HDCA was reviewed and strengthened by the Online Safety Act 2021.
laws.penalty: Criminal HDCA offense: up to 2 years imprisonment; civil orders requiring takedown
exceptions: News media reporting in public interest
Academic and educational use of harmful content

quiz.q: What government-approved agency provides mediation under New Zealand's Harmful Digital Communications Act?
quiz.explanation: NetSafe is the government-approved agency that provides the first-response service for the Harmful Digital Communications Act, offering complaint intake, advice, and mediation before matters escalate to police or civil courts.

laws.title: Reserve Bank Act 2021 / Monetary Policy
laws.subtitle: RBNZ independence and financial stability
laws.fullDescription: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand Act 2021 reformed the governance of the central bank, establishing an externally appointed Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) to set interest rates. The RBNZ has a dual mandate: price stability (1-3% inflation) and maximum sustainable employment. The rapid rise of interest rates in 2022-2023 (from 0.25% to 5.5%) caused significant mortgage stress for heavily indebted New Zealand households.
laws.penalty: No criminal penalties for monetary policy decisions; RBNZ has prudential supervision powers
exceptions: Minister of Finance can give policy directions in extraordinary circumstances
Deposit protection scheme (NZ$100,000) established

quiz.q: What is the Reserve Bank of New Zealand's inflation target band?
quiz.explanation: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand targets consumer price inflation within a band of 1-3%, with a focus on keeping inflation near the 2% midpoint, under the remit set by the Minister of Finance.

laws.title: GI Protection / Kiwifruit and Manuka
laws.subtitle: Geographical indications and primary sector law
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand's primary sector is economically critical — dairy (Fonterra), kiwifruit (Zespri), meat, and seafood are major exports. Disputes over geographical indications include the international 'manuka honey' trademark fight between NZ and Australian beekeepers. Zespri monopoly on kiwifruit exports has been challenged legally. The Food Safety Act 2014 governs food standards aligned with Food Standards Australia New Zealand (FSANZ).
laws.penalty: Food safety violations: significant fines; fraudulent GI labeling: Trade Marks Act penalties
exceptions: Backyard beekeeping has different registration requirements
Farmers markets have modified food safety rules

quiz.q: Which NZ export cooperative holds a statutory monopoly on kiwifruit exports?
quiz.explanation: Zespri holds a statutory monopoly on kiwifruit exports from New Zealand under the Kiwifruit Export Regulations, meaning all New Zealand kiwifruit for export must be marketed through Zespri's marketing system.

laws.title: Police Act 2008 / Policing Ethics
laws.subtitle: Police accountability and oversight
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand Police operate under the Policing Act 2008, which emphasizes community policing and collaboration. The Independent Police Conduct Authority (IPCA) investigates complaints against police. New Zealand's police are generally unarmed (carrying firearms only in special circumstances). The Police Association has opposed routinely arming police despite a 6-month pilot in 2019-2020. Police response to Christchurch attack in 2019 was praised for speed.
laws.penalty: Police misconduct: IPCA investigation; criminal charges for officer misconduct
exceptions: Armed offenders squad carries firearms
Special tactical units maintain weapons

quiz.q: Do New Zealand police routinely carry firearms?
options: No — generally unarmed except in special circumstances
Only when responding to armed offender calls
quiz.explanation: New Zealand Police are generally unarmed — they do not routinely carry firearms on patrol, instead keeping weapons secured in police vehicles for access when needed. A 2019-2020 pilot of routine arming was ended after most officers opposed making it permanent.

laws.title: Social Security Act 2018 / Welfare Reform
laws.subtitle: Benefit system and welfare policy
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand's Social Security Act 2018 consolidated welfare legislation. Benefits include Jobseeker Support, Sole Parent Support, Supported Living Payment, and New Zealand Superannuation (universal pension at 65, no means test). National Superannuation is paid to all NZ residents aged 65+ regardless of wealth — a universal pension that critics argue is unsustainable. The Welfare Expert Advisory Group (2019) recommended significant welfare reforms.
laws.penalty: Benefit fraud: criminal prosecution; recovery of overpayments
exceptions: 65+ universal superannuation regardless of other income
Accommodation Supplement to help with housing costs

quiz.q: What is unique about New Zealand's National Superannuation pension for those aged 65+?
options: It is universal — paid regardless of wealth or other income
It is only available to NZ citizens
quiz.explanation: New Zealand's National Superannuation is a universal pension paid to all residents aged 65 and over regardless of their other income or savings, making it one of the most universally accessible pension systems in the developed world.

laws.title: Voluntary Assisted Dying Act 2019
laws.subtitle: End of life choice in NZ
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand's End of Life Choice Act 2019 was approved by 65.1% of voters in a binding referendum held alongside the 2020 general election. Assisted dying became available from 7 November 2021 for terminally ill adults with a life expectancy of 6 months or less. New Zealand has strong safeguards including dual doctor approval and a 10-day waiting period. The law allows people to self-administer or have a doctor administer the lethal medication.
laws.penalty: Assisted dying outside the legal framework: criminal prosecution
exceptions: Conscientious objection allows doctors to decline participation
Must refer to a willing doctor if declining
laws.sourceLabel: NZ Ministry of Health End of Life Choice

quiz.q: What percentage of voters approved New Zealand's End of Life Choice Act in the 2020 referendum?
quiz.explanation: New Zealand's End of Life Choice Act was approved by 65.1% of voters in a binding referendum held alongside the October 2020 general election, with assisted dying becoming available from 7 November 2021.

laws.title: Dairy Industry Restructuring Act 2001 / Fonterra
laws.subtitle: Fonterra and dairy export dominance
laws.fullDescription: The Dairy Industry Restructuring Act 2001 created Fonterra — the global dairy giant owned by NZ dairy farmers — through a merger of New Zealand's major dairy cooperatives. Fonterra accounts for approximately 30% of the world's internationally traded dairy products. Fonterra's 2013 botulism scare (later found to be false) disrupted NZ's dairy trade and damaged international reputation. The company has restructured repeatedly to address profitability concerns.
laws.penalty: DIRA compliance: regulatory sanctions; competition law for Fonterra's dominant position
exceptions: Co-operative structure means farmer-owners have special governance rights
Raw milk access regime for independent processors

quiz.q: Approximately what percentage of the world's internationally traded dairy products does Fonterra account for?
quiz.explanation: Fonterra accounts for approximately 30% of the world's internationally traded dairy products, making it the world's largest dairy exporter and a dominant force in global dairy markets.

laws.title: Terrorism — Christchurch Attack / Sentencing
laws.subtitle: The 2019 attacks and terrorism sentencing
laws.fullDescription: The Christchurch mosque attacks on 15 March 2019 killed 51 people and injured 40 in what was New Zealand's deadliest peacetime mass murder. Brenton Tarrant pleaded guilty to 51 counts of murder, 40 counts of attempted murder, and one terrorism charge. In August 2020, he received life imprisonment without parole — the first such sentence in New Zealand history, requiring specific amendment of the Sentencing Act.
laws.penalty: Terrorism with murder: life imprisonment without parole (first time used in NZ history)
exceptions: No exceptions — life without parole is final

quiz.q: What was historically significant about the sentencing of the Christchurch mosque attacker?
options: He was the youngest person sentenced to life in NZ
He received the first death sentence in 40 years
He received the first life without parole sentence in NZ history
He was tried in an international court
quiz.explanation: Brenton Tarrant's August 2020 sentencing to life imprisonment without the possibility of parole was the first time this sentence had ever been imposed in New Zealand, requiring a specific amendment to the Sentencing Act.

laws.title: Conservation Act 1987 / DOC
laws.subtitle: Department of Conservation and predator free NZ
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand's Conservation Act 1987 established the Department of Conservation (DOC) to manage protected areas and native species. NZ's biodiversity crisis — introduced predators (rats, stoats, possums) threaten endemic species including kiwi — has led to the ambitious Predator Free 2050 goal to eradicate all introduced mammalian predators from NZ by 2050. Aerial 1080 (sodium fluoroacetate) drops are the primary pest control tool, though controversial.
laws.penalty: Killing protected native species: up to NZ$100,000 fine; 1080 unauthorized use: criminal offense
exceptions: DOC and licensed operators can use 1080 for pest control
Scientific research permits for handling native species

quiz.q: What is New Zealand's ambitious goal regarding introduced mammalian predators by 2050?
options: Control predators in all national parks
Eradicate all introduced mammalian predators from NZ
quiz.explanation: New Zealand's Predator Free 2050 program has the ambitious goal of eradicating all introduced mammalian predators (rats, stoats, and possums) from New Zealand by 2050, to protect and restore the country's unique endemic wildlife.

laws.title: Human Rights Act 1993 / Privacy
laws.subtitle: Human rights and discrimination law
laws.fullDescription: The Human Rights Act 1993 prohibits discrimination in employment and access to goods, services, and facilities on grounds including race, sex, pregnancy, religious belief, disability, sexual orientation, and age. The Human Rights Commission provides education and complaints resolution. New Zealand's human rights protections are generally considered strong, though gaps exist in enforcement mechanisms. The HRA and NZBORA work alongside each other.
laws.penalty: Human rights violations: Human Rights Tribunal orders; compensation
exceptions: Religious bodies have limited exemptions for employment based on faith
Competitive sport has exemptions for age and sex

quiz.q: What body hears complaints under New Zealand's Human Rights Act?
quiz.explanation: The Human Rights Review Tribunal hears and determines complaints under the Human Rights Act 1993 that cannot be resolved through the Human Rights Commission's mediation processes.

laws.title: Infrastructure Funding and Financing Act 2020
laws.subtitle: Infrastructure investment and housing development
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand's Infrastructure Funding and Financing Act 2020 created a new model for financing infrastructure for housing developments — through 'special purpose vehicles' that levy charges on properties benefiting from the infrastructure over 30+ years. This 'infrastructure levy' model aims to unlock housing development by removing upfront infrastructure cost barriers. New Zealand faces a significant infrastructure deficit due to decades of underinvestment.
laws.penalty: Non-payment of infrastructure levies: charged against land title
exceptions: Existing residents on developed land not subject to new levies
Government can provide grants alongside levy funding

quiz.q: What new financing mechanism did NZ's 2020 Infrastructure Funding and Financing Act create?
options: Infrastructure bonds issued by local councils
Special purpose vehicles collecting levies over 30+ years
Direct Treasury grants for housing infrastructure
quiz.explanation: The Infrastructure Funding and Financing Act 2020 created a mechanism using special purpose vehicles (SPVs) to finance infrastructure for housing developments, with the cost recovered through levies on benefiting properties over 30-50 years.

laws.title: Sale and Supply of Alcohol Act 2012
laws.subtitle: Alcohol licensing and harm reduction
laws.fullDescription: The Sale and Supply of Alcohol Act 2012 reformed NZ's liquor licensing system, establishing District Licensing Committees and the Alcohol Regulatory and Licensing Authority. NZ has relatively high rates of alcohol harm — the default on-license closing time of 4am has been challenged. The Alcohol Act allows communities to set local alcohol policies. Licensed premises must not supply to intoxicated persons.
laws.penalty: Supplying to minors: up to NZ$25,000; supplying to intoxicated person: up to NZ$10,000
exceptions: Parents can supply alcohol to their own minor children
Marae and community events have modified licensing

quiz.q: What default closing time do on-licenses (bars) have under NZ's Sale and Supply of Alcohol Act 2012?
quiz.explanation: The default maximum closing time for on-licenses (bars, restaurants, clubs) under the Sale and Supply of Alcohol Act 2012 is 4am, though Local Alcohol Policies can set earlier closing times for areas experiencing alcohol-related harm.

laws.title: Care of Children Act 2004 / Family Court
laws.subtitle: Child custody and family law
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand's Care of Children Act 2004 governs parenting orders and guardianship. The Family Court handles relationship property division (under the Property (Relationships) Act 1976), child custody, and domestic violence protection orders. The Hague Convention on International Child Abduction applies to cross-border parenting disputes. New Zealand has a specialist Family Violence Court in some areas.
laws.penalty: Breaching parenting orders: contempt of court; international abduction: criminal offense
exceptions: Urgent without-notice orders available in immediate danger
Cultural considerations in some guardianship disputes

quiz.q: What Act governs the division of relationship property when couples separate in New Zealand?
quiz.explanation: The Property (Relationships) Act 1976 governs the division of property when married couples, civil union partners, or de facto partners (of 3+ years) separate in New Zealand, with a general principle of equal sharing of relationship property.

laws.title: Aid and Development / Pacific Partnerships
laws.subtitle: MFAT aid programme and Pacific engagement
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand's development assistance program — managed by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade (MFAT) — focuses primarily on the Pacific, with over 60% of aid going to Pacific Island nations. NZ also contributes to multilateral development banks and UN agencies. Pacific engagement includes disaster relief (Cyclone Gabrielle 2023), infrastructure investment, and education scholarships. Climate financing is an increasing component of NZ's Pacific development assistance.
laws.penalty: Aid misappropriation by recipients: contract termination; New Zealand law applies to NZ officials
exceptions: Multilateral contributions follow organizational rules
Budget support sometimes provided directly to governments

quiz.q: What percentage of NZ's foreign aid goes to Pacific Island nations?
quiz.explanation: Over 60% of New Zealand's official development assistance (aid) goes to Pacific Island nations, reflecting NZ's close geographic, cultural, and political ties with the Pacific and its recognition of climate-related development challenges there.

laws.title: Education and Training Act 2020
laws.subtitle: Compulsory education and tertiary system
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand's Education and Training Act 2020 governs schooling from early childhood to tertiary level. Schooling is compulsory from ages 6-16 (attending from 5 is near-universal). NZ has strong PISA rankings in some areas. Tertiary education is managed through Tertiary Education Commission (TEC) funding. The student loan scheme is similar to Australia's HECS, repayable once earning over NZ$22,828/year. Teacher shortages are a significant challenge.
laws.penalty: Non-enrollment of school-age children: prosecution of parents; truancy: school and government intervention
exceptions: Home schooling is permitted with MOE notification
Overseas students in NZ have different enrollment rules

quiz.q: At what age is school attendance compulsory in New Zealand?
quiz.explanation: School attendance is compulsory in New Zealand from age 6 to 16 under the Education and Training Act 2020, though virtually all children start at age 5, when school enrollment becomes available.

laws.title: Biosecurity Act 1993 / Kauri Dieback
laws.subtitle: Biosecurity and invasive species
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand's Biosecurity Act 1993 is one of the world's most comprehensive biosecurity frameworks, reflecting NZ's unique biodiversity. Kauri dieback disease (Phytophthora agathidicida) threatens NZ's iconic kauri trees — some access to kauri forests has been restricted. Myrtle rust threatens pohutukawa and rata trees. The National Pest Management Plans target possums, rabbits, and other agricultural pests.
laws.penalty: Deliberate introduction of pests: criminal prosecution; failure to comply with inspection: fines
exceptions: Scientific research with containment approval
Approved biocontrol agents

quiz.q: What disease is threatening New Zealand's iconic kauri trees?
quiz.explanation: Kauri dieback, caused by the water mold Phytophthora agathidicida, is threatening New Zealand's iconic kauri trees (some over 1,000 years old) by attacking roots and preventing water and nutrient uptake. Cleaning footwear before entering kauri forests is mandatory.

laws.title: Parliamentary Privilege / Standing Orders
laws.subtitle: Parliamentary rules and privilege
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand's parliamentary privilege allows MPs to speak freely in the House without legal liability (civil or criminal) for what they say during proceedings. Standing Orders govern how Parliament operates — debating rules, select committees, and quorum requirements. The Speaker maintains order. The Epidemic Preparedness Act 2006 allows COVID-type emergency legislative procedures. Parliament met virtually for the first time during COVID-19.
laws.penalty: Contempt of Parliament: rare; Speaker can have members removed
exceptions: Privilege does not extend to MPs' actions outside parliament
Select committee proceedings also privileged

quiz.q: What protection does parliamentary privilege provide to NZ Members of Parliament?
options: Freedom to speak in Parliament without civil or criminal liability for those statements
Right to refuse to appear in court
quiz.explanation: Parliamentary privilege protects NZ MPs from civil or criminal liability for anything said during parliamentary proceedings, allowing free debate without fear of defamation suits or other legal consequences for in-Parliament statements.

laws.title: Electricity Industry Act 2010 / Renewable Energy
laws.subtitle: NZ electricity market and renewable generation
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand generates approximately 85% of its electricity from renewable sources, primarily hydroelectric (South Island lakes), geothermal, and wind. The Electricity Industry Act 2010 governs the competitive wholesale and retail electricity market. Lake levels — particularly at Lake Pukaki and Lake Tekapo — are watched closely as hydro determines spot electricity prices. NZ's electricity system was stressed by the 2021 'hydro dry year' gas shortage crisis.
laws.penalty: Electricity market manipulation: Electricity Authority fines
exceptions: Transpower (grid operator) has regulated returns
Small-scale embedded generation (solar, community) has lighter regulations

quiz.q: Approximately what percentage of New Zealand's electricity comes from renewable sources?
quiz.explanation: New Zealand generates approximately 85% of its electricity from renewable sources, primarily hydroelectric power, geothermal energy, and wind power, making it one of the most renewable electricity systems in the developed world.

laws.title: Defamation Act 1992 / NZ Media Law
laws.subtitle: Defamation and press freedom
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand's Defamation Act 1992 provides for civil claims for defamatory publications. Truth is a complete defense. Qualified privilege protects fair reports of parliamentary and court proceedings. New Zealand has a relatively small, concentrated media market. The 2023 establishment of Stuff Ltd (previously owned by Nine Entertainment Australia) as a journalist-owned cooperative was a globally unusual media transition.
laws.penalty: Defamation: civil damages (no cap); no criminal defamation in NZ
exceptions: Parliamentary privilege protects statements in Parliament
Fair comment on matters of public interest

quiz.q: What unusual transition did New Zealand media company Stuff undergo in 2020-2023?
options: It was nationalized by the government
quiz.explanation: Stuff Ltd (NZ's largest newspaper publisher) became a journalist-owned cooperative in 2020 when CEO Sinead Boucher purchased it from Nine Entertainment for NZ$1, creating one of the world's most unusual media ownership structures.

laws.title: Secret Commissions Act 1910 / Bribery
laws.subtitle: Anti-bribery law and public integrity
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand's anti-corruption framework includes the Secret Commissions Act 1910, the Crimes Act (bribery provisions), and the Local Authorities (Members Interests) Act 1968. NZ consistently ranks in the top 3 of Transparency International's CPI. Public officials have strong obligations to declare conflicts of interest. The NZ Police investigate corruption and the SFO handles serious financial crime. NZ has benefited from a relatively small, close-knit public sector.
laws.penalty: Bribery of officials: up to 14 years imprisonment
exceptions: Gifts under specified thresholds may be accepted (varies by agency)
Facilitation payments are treated as bribery

quiz.q: How does New Zealand typically rank globally on anti-corruption indices?
quiz.explanation: New Zealand consistently ranks in the top 3 least corrupt countries globally on Transparency International's Corruption Perceptions Index, alongside Denmark and Finland, reflecting strong public sector integrity.

laws.title: Land Transport Act 1998 / Road Safety
laws.subtitle: Traffic law and drunk driving
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand's Land Transport Act 1998 governs road use, including one of the world's lowest drink-drive limits (0.05 BAC for those over 20; zero for under 20s and commercial drivers). Road deaths remain a significant concern — NZ has a relatively high road fatality rate per capita for a developed country. Speed camera enforcement, drug driving testing, and distracted driving laws have been strengthened. The rural road toll is disproportionately high.
laws.penalty: Driving over 0.05 BAC: infringement; over 0.08: criminal offense up to 3 months imprisonment
exceptions: Special test for under-20s: zero alcohol tolerance
Commercial drivers have stricter limits

quiz.q: What blood alcohol concentration (BAC) limit applies to drivers over 20 in New Zealand?
quiz.explanation: New Zealand's drink-drive limit for drivers over 20 is 0.05 BAC (equivalent to approximately one drink for most people), which is lower than the 0.08 limit in many countries. Under-20s and commercial drivers have a zero-alcohol limit.

laws.title: Disinformation / Online Safety and AI
laws.subtitle: Online safety and emerging technology
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand's Online Safety Act 2022 reformed the Broadcasting Act to cover online content services. NZ has been active globally on disinformation — the Christchurch Call's tech company commitments extend to non-terrorist harmful content. The DIA (Department of Internal Affairs) regulates online gambling and harmful digital content. NZ participated in the AI Safety Summit (Bletchley, 2023) and signed the international AI safety statement.
laws.penalty: Online safety violations by platforms: infringement notices; serious violations: civil penalties
exceptions: News media and user-generated content have different treatment
Research and journalism exemptions

quiz.q: What government department regulates online safety and gambling in New Zealand?
quiz.explanation: The Department of Internal Affairs (DIA) in New Zealand regulates online safety matters including harmful online content, online gambling, and classification of publications and films.

laws.title: Pae Ora Healthy Futures Act 2022
laws.subtitle: Health system reform and equity
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand's Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) Act 2022 established the new health system with Health New Zealand (Te Whatu Ora) replacing the 20 District Health Boards. Pae Ora means 'healthy futures' in Māori and reflects the government's commitment to equity in health outcomes. The legislation includes specific focus on Māori, Pacific peoples, and other population groups with poorer health outcomes. NZ's health system performs well on international comparisons but inequities persist.
laws.penalty: Health service provider breaches: professional regulatory action; serious safety violations: criminal prosecution
exceptions: Private health insurance supplements public system
Accident Compensation (ACC) covers accident treatment separately

quiz.q: What does Pae Ora mean in Māori?
quiz.explanation: Pae Ora means 'healthy futures' in Te Reo Māori. The Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) Act 2022 established New Zealand's new health system under Health New Zealand (Te Whatu Ora), with a focus on health equity.

laws.title: Reserve Bank Act 2021 / Bank Capital
laws.subtitle: Financial stability and bank regulation
laws.fullDescription: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand (RBNZ) under the Reserve Bank Act 2021 regulates banks, insurance companies, and non-bank deposit takers. The RBNZ increased bank capital requirements significantly (2019 reforms, 2021 Act), requiring big banks to hold more equity capital over 7 years. NZ's banking sector is dominated by Australian-owned banks (ANZ, ASB/CBA, BNZ/NAB, Westpac), raising concerns about financial stability in a crisis.
laws.penalty: Prudential breaches: RBNZ directions; systematic failure: intervention powers
exceptions: Registered banks must hold minimum capital ratios
Non-bank deposit takers have different requirements

quiz.q: What nationality owns most of New Zealand's major banks?
quiz.explanation: New Zealand's four largest banks — ANZ, ASB (owned by CBA), BNZ (owned by NAB), and Westpac — are all majority-owned by Australian banking groups, raising financial stability concerns about NZ's dependence on foreign-owned banking.

laws.title: NZ Refugee Quota / UNHCR Resettlement
laws.subtitle: Refugee resettlement programme
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand accepts refugees through the UNHCR resettlement program — the annual quota was doubled from 750 to 1,500 in 2020. NZ also accepts Convention refugees who arrive independently and claim asylum, though numbers are small given geographic isolation. New Zealand has accepted Syrian, Congolese, Bhutanese, and other refugee populations. The Rainbow Tick resettlement program recognizes LGBTQ+ refugee needs.
laws.penalty: Refugee fraud: deportation; immigration crimes: criminal prosecution
exceptions: Convention refugees cannot be returned to persecution
Family reunification for recognized refugees available

quiz.q: What is New Zealand's annual refugee resettlement quota (as increased in 2020)?
quiz.explanation: New Zealand's annual UNHCR resettlement quota was doubled from 750 to 1,500 in 2020, responding to calls to increase NZ's contribution to global refugee resettlement and reflecting the country's broader international commitments.

laws.title: Computer Crimes Act / Cybersecurity NZ
laws.subtitle: Cybercrime and GCSB
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand's Crimes Act 1961 contains computer offence provisions (Crimes Amendment Act 2003) covering unauthorized access, interference, and interception. The GCSB (Government Communications Security Bureau) provides cybersecurity support to critical national infrastructure through its NCSC (National Cyber Security Centre). High-profile cyberattacks on NZ Stock Exchange (2020) and healthcare sector demonstrated vulnerabilities. NZ is part of the Five Eyes cybersharing network.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized access to computer systems: up to 2 years; interference: up to 10 years
exceptions: Authorized penetration testing and security research
Intelligence agencies operating under warrant

quiz.q: What is the GCSB's cybersecurity unit that supports critical national infrastructure called?
quiz.explanation: The GCSB's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) provides cybersecurity advice and assistance to the New Zealand government and critical national infrastructure, and monitors and responds to significant cyber threats.

laws.title: Resource Management Amendment Act 2023 / Housing
laws.subtitle: RMA fast-track and housing intensification
laws.fullDescription: After years of failed attempts to reform the Resource Management Act (RMA), the National-led government (2023) passed the Fast-track Approvals Act 2024, creating a ministerial expert panel process to streamline consents for significant infrastructure and housing projects. The prior Labour government had passed the Natural and Built Environment Act and Spatial Planning Act (2023) to replace the RMA, which National repealed. NZ continues to struggle with housing supply.
laws.penalty: RMA breaches: fines, enforcement orders; non-compliance with fast-track conditions: project revocation
exceptions: Nationally significant infrastructure (roads, energy) has separate designation process
Existing resource consents remain valid

quiz.q: What did the National government repeal in 2023 that the Labour government had passed to replace the RMA?
options: The Natural and Built Environment Act and Spatial Planning Act
quiz.explanation: The National-led government repealed the Natural and Built Environment Act (NBA) and Spatial Planning Act (SPA) passed by Labour in 2023 to replace the RMA, reverting to the original RMA while fast-tracking a new reform process.

laws.title: Jacinda Ardern / Leadership and Maternity
laws.subtitle: First elected leader to give birth in office
laws.fullDescription: Jacinda Ardern, New Zealand's 40th Prime Minister (2017-2023), became the second elected world leader in history to give birth while in office (2018). She brought her baby to the UN General Assembly. Ardern was known for empathetic leadership during the Christchurch attacks and COVID-19. She resigned in January 2023, citing the toll on her wellbeing — sparking global debate about sustainability of political leadership. Chris Hipkins succeeded her.
laws.penalty: No legal provisions; leadership decisions not subject to criminal law
exceptions: Prime Minister has legal immunities in official capacity
Parliamentary Speaker manages parliamentary procedures

quiz.q: What historical milestone did Jacinda Ardern achieve in 2018?
options: First woman Prime Minister of NZ
Second elected world leader to give birth while in office
First NZ PM to address the UN
quiz.explanation: Jacinda Ardern became the second elected world leader in history to give birth while in office in June 2018 (after Pakistan's Benazir Bhutto in 1990), and notably brought her infant to the UN General Assembly.

laws.title: Gambling Act 2003 / Problem Gambling
laws.subtitle: Lotteries, pokies and harm minimisation
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand's Gambling Act 2003 classifies gambling activities and provides harm minimization frameworks. The Gambling Harm Reduction Act restricts the number of gaming machines (pokies) in communities — numbers have been decreasing. Casino gambling is permitted at SkyCity Auckland and other casinos. Problem gambling support services are funded by levies on gambling operators. Online gambling by offshore operators to NZ residents is regulated but enforcement is limited.
laws.penalty: Unlicensed gambling operations: up to NZ$20,000 fine; organised crime gambling: criminal prosecution
exceptions: Class 1 gambling (small prizes) needs no license
Lottery games run by Lotteries Commission under separate rules

quiz.q: Which major casino complex in Auckland is a significant gambling venue in New Zealand?
quiz.explanation: SkyCity Auckland is New Zealand's largest casino and entertainment complex, located in central Auckland adjacent to the Sky Tower. SkyCity also operates casinos in Hamilton and Queenstown.

laws.title: NZ and Pacific Island Law Enforcement
laws.subtitle: Pacific policing and border security
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand has close law enforcement cooperation with Pacific Island nations, providing policing support to the Cook Islands (which is in free association with NZ), Niue, and Tokelau (NZ territories). The Pacific Policing Initiative (2024) formalizes cooperation. Methamphetamine trafficking from Asia through the Pacific to NZ is a major challenge. NZ Customs and police cooperate with Pacific Island counterparts on drug smuggling and human trafficking.
laws.penalty: Drug trafficking: imprisonment; people smuggling: up to 20 years
exceptions: Cook Islands, Niue, and Tokelau citizens are NZ citizens
PICTA (Pacific Island Countries Trade Agreement) includes some security cooperation

quiz.q: Which Pacific territories are in free association with New Zealand, whose citizens are also NZ citizens?
quiz.explanation: The Cook Islands and Niue are self-governing states in free association with New Zealand, meaning their citizens are also New Zealand citizens with the right to live and work in NZ. Tokelau is a non-self-governing NZ territory.

laws.title: National Climate Change Risk Assessment
laws.subtitle: Climate adaptation and flood risk
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand's first National Climate Change Risk Assessment (2020) identified the 43 most significant climate risks, including flooding, coastal inundation, drought, and loss of biodiversity. Cyclone Gabrielle (February 2023) — NZ's costliest natural disaster — devastated Hawke's Bay and Northland, causing NZ$14.5 billion in damage. NZ's managed retreat policy (moving communities away from flood-prone areas) is politically contentious but increasingly necessary.
laws.penalty: Building on flood-prone or coastal land contrary to climate risk plans: refusal of consent; potential future loss of insurance
exceptions: Existing development rights subject to transition provisions
Māori land has separate consultation requirements

quiz.q: Which 2023 cyclone was New Zealand's costliest natural disaster?
quiz.explanation: Cyclone Gabrielle struck New Zealand in February 2023, becoming the country's costliest natural disaster with estimated damage of NZ$14.5 billion, devastating Hawke's Bay, Northland, and other regions.

laws.title: Health and Safety at Work Act 2015
laws.subtitle: WorkSafe and workplace safety
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand's Health and Safety at Work Act 2015 (inspired by the Pike River Mine disaster of 2010, which killed 29 miners) places primary duty of care on Persons Conducting Business or Undertakings (PCBUs). WorkSafe NZ is the primary regulator. Worker health and safety representatives have specific rights. NZ has improved its workplace fatality rate since the legislation but fatalities in high-risk industries (farming, logging, construction) remain a concern.
laws.penalty: Serious H&S failures: up to NZ$3 million for organizations; up to NZ$600,000 for individuals or 5 years imprisonment
exceptions: Volunteer organizations have modified obligations
Home-based childcare has specific safety standards

quiz.q: What disaster directly inspired the reform of NZ's workplace safety law with the Health and Safety at Work Act 2015?
quiz.explanation: The Pike River Mine disaster of November 2010, in which 29 miners died in a methane explosion, directly led to the overhaul of New Zealand's workplace safety legislation, resulting in the Health and Safety at Work Act 2015.

laws.title: Supreme Court Act 2003 / Privy Council
laws.subtitle: NZ Supreme Court and final appeal
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand's Supreme Court was established by the Supreme Court Act 2003, replacing the Privy Council in London as NZ's final court of appeal from 1 January 2004. The change was controversial — the Privy Council had provided a perceived independence and international perspective. The Supreme Court has 5 judges and sits in Wellington. High-profile decisions include the Urewera case (2012) and climate/environment cases.
laws.penalty: No direct penalties; Supreme Court decisions are binding on all lower courts
exceptions: Certain criminal appeals not available to Supreme Court
Leave to appeal required

quiz.q: What court did the NZ Supreme Court (established 2004) replace as New Zealand's final court of appeal?
quiz.explanation: New Zealand's Supreme Court, established by the Supreme Court Act 2003 and sitting from 1 January 2004, replaced the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in London as New Zealand's final court of appeal.

laws.title: Disability (Increasing Participation) Act 2023
laws.subtitle: Disability rights and CRPD
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand ratified the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD) in 2008. The Disability Action Plan 2019-2023 sets goals for participation and inclusion. New Zealand has high rates of disability — approximately 24% of the population has some form of disability. The Enabling Good Lives approach (piloted in several regions) aims to give disabled people more choice and control over their support.
