laws.penalty: Disability discrimination in employment: Employment Relations Authority; service access: Human Rights Act proceedings
exceptions: ACC covers disability resulting from accidents (separate funding)
Education system has modified obligations for different types of disability

quiz.q: Approximately what percentage of New Zealand's population has some form of disability?
quiz.explanation: Approximately 24% of New Zealand's population has some form of disability, one of the higher rates among OECD countries, reflecting broad definitions and an aging population.

laws.title: Fiscal Responsibility Act / Wellbeing Budget
laws.subtitle: NZ economic policy and wellbeing indicators
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand's Public Finance Act 1989 and the Fiscal Responsibility Act established fiscal responsibility principles. The Wellbeing Budget, introduced by Finance Minister Grant Robertson in 2019, allocated funding based on wellbeing outcomes (mental health, child poverty, Māori and Pacific wellbeing, climate) rather than purely GDP measures. This 'wellbeing economics' approach was widely studied globally but has been scaled back by the National government.
laws.penalty: No direct penalties; fiscal responsibility principles enforced through parliamentary accountability
exceptions: Emergencies can override fiscal responsibility targets
Capital investment is treated differently from operating expenditure

quiz.q: What innovative budget approach did New Zealand introduce in 2019 that attracted global attention?
quiz.explanation: New Zealand's Wellbeing Budget (2019) allocated government funding based on wellbeing outcomes rather than purely GDP metrics, becoming globally influential as an example of 'wellbeing economics' applied to national fiscal policy.

laws.title: Primary Industries Law / Fisheries
laws.subtitle: Quota Management System and fisheries
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand's Quota Management System (QMS), introduced in 1986, is one of the world's first large-scale individual transferable quota (ITQ) fisheries management systems. Fishing companies own tradeable quota to catch specific fish species. The system has been credited with stabilizing fish stocks but criticized for concentrating quota ownership in large corporations. Māori customary fishing rights (managed under the Treaty of Waitangi Fisheries Claims Settlement Act 1992) coexist.
laws.penalty: Fishing over quota: license suspension; serious fishing violations: criminal prosecution and quota forfeiture
exceptions: Customary fishing permits for Māori
Amateur fishing limits separate from commercial QMS

quiz.q: What was innovative about New Zealand's Quota Management System introduced in 1986?
options: It was one of the world's first individual transferable quota (ITQ) fisheries systems
It gave all fishing rights to Māori
It created a government fishing monopoly
quiz.explanation: New Zealand's Quota Management System (1986) was one of the world's first large-scale individual transferable quota (ITQ) fisheries management systems, allowing companies to buy, sell, and trade quota units, creating market incentives for sustainable fishing.

laws.title: Sensitive Claims / Mental Health ACC
laws.subtitle: ACC and sexual abuse and mental injury
laws.fullDescription: ACC covers sensitive claims — personal injury from sexual abuse or assault — alongside physical injuries. The process for sensitive claims is tailored to survivors' needs, with trauma-informed assessors and specially trained staff. NZ's ACC coverage of mental injury from criminal acts (e.g., PTSD from witnessing violence) was expanded. The ACC scheme is funded by levies on employers, employees, and motor vehicle registration — not general taxation.
laws.penalty: Providing false information to ACC for claims: criminal prosecution
exceptions: Mental injury from traumatic events now covered
Work injuries have employer levy funding; road injuries have motor vehicle levy

quiz.q: What types of injuries does ACC's 'sensitive claims' process cover?
options: Personal injury from sexual abuse or assault
quiz.explanation: ACC's 'sensitive claims' process covers personal injury (including psychological injury) resulting from sexual abuse or sexual assault, with specialized trauma-informed staff and processes to support survivors through their claims.

laws.title: Animal Welfare Act 1999
laws.subtitle: Animal protection and NZ law
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand's Animal Welfare Act 1999 sets standards for animal care, prohibiting unnecessary suffering, and governs research using animals (including the '3Rs' — replace, reduce, refine). NZ has progressive protections — great apes are recognized as sentient beings with special protections. Farm animal welfare standards are a growing area with consumer and export market interest. NZ's position as an agricultural exporter makes animal welfare commercially significant.
laws.penalty: Wilful ill-treatment of animals: up to NZ$75,000 fine or 3 years imprisonment
exceptions: Farming practices deemed acceptable under codes of welfare
Pest control with approved methods

quiz.q: What special legal protections do great apes receive under NZ's animal welfare framework?
options: They are protected as endangered species only
They are recognized as sentient beings with specific legal protections
They have the same rights as domestic pets
There are no specific protections for great apes
quiz.explanation: New Zealand's Animal Welfare Act recognizes great apes (chimpanzees, gorillas, orangutans, bonobos) as sentient beings with special protections, prohibiting their use in research, testing, or teaching except in their best interests.

laws.title: Official Information Act 1982 (OIA)
laws.subtitle: Government transparency and public access
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand's Official Information Act 1982 gives citizens the right to request official information from government agencies. It operates on a presumption of disclosure — the default is openness, with specified grounds for withholding (national security, personal privacy, commercial sensitivity). The Ombudsman can investigate refusals and recommend release. NZ consistently rates highly for government transparency. The OIA has revealed sensitive information about COVID-19 decisions, intelligence, and Treaty claims.
laws.penalty: Withholding information unlawfully: Ombudsman can recommend disclosure; no direct criminal penalties
exceptions: Cabinet documents and security information can be withheld
Personal information about third parties protected

quiz.q: What is the foundational principle of New Zealand's Official Information Act 1982?
options: Information is property of the Crown
Presumption of disclosure (openness is the default)
Citizens must demonstrate need to access information
quiz.explanation: The Official Information Act 1982 operates on a 'presumption of disclosure' — government agencies must release information unless they can demonstrate specific grounds for withholding it, making openness the default rather than the exception.

laws.title: NZ Global Talent Visa / Skilled Migration
laws.subtitle: Talent attraction and immigration
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand's Skilled Migrant Category and Global Visa programme aim to attract skilled workers and entrepreneurs. NZ faces a significant emigration challenge — young, educated New Zealanders leaving for higher wages in Australia (NZ citizens can live and work in Australia freely). Labour shortages across healthcare, construction, and technology have driven immigration policy reforms. The 2023 immigration rebalance aimed to attract higher-skill migrants.
laws.penalty: Immigration fraud: criminal prosecution; misrepresenting skills: visa cancellation
exceptions: Global Talent Visa (Green List) fast-tracks certain skills
Returning NZ citizens have unconditional entry

quiz.q: What advantage do NZ citizens have in Australia that contributes to NZ's emigration challenge?
options: Free right to live and work in Australia without a visa
Australian citizenship automatically granted after 5 years
quiz.explanation: New Zealand citizens can live and work in Australia without requiring a visa under the Trans-Tasman Travel Arrangement, creating a constant 'brain drain' as young, skilled New Zealanders move to Australia for higher wages.

laws.title: Electricity Pricing / Low Income Households
laws.subtitle: Electricity affordability and fuel poverty
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand faces significant electricity affordability challenges despite having cheap generation — the retail market has been criticized for high consumer prices. Energy hardship (inability to adequately heat homes) affects an estimated 100,000+ households. NZ's old, leaky housing stock exacerbates energy poverty. The Electricity Price Review (2019) found the market structure disadvantages consumers. Decarbonizing heating (moving from gas to electricity) is a major policy challenge.
laws.penalty: Electricity theft: criminal prosecution; failure to meet consumer guarantee standards: Commerce Commission action
exceptions: Low User Tariff for small consumers (below 8,000 kWh/year)
Metering exemptions for remote areas

quiz.q: How many NZ households are estimated to experience energy hardship (fuel poverty)?
quiz.explanation: An estimated 100,000+ New Zealand households experience energy hardship — unable to adequately heat their homes due to cost — driven by high electricity prices, low incomes, and poor-quality housing stock.

laws.title: New Zealand Race Relations Act 1971
laws.subtitle: Race relations and multicultural society
laws.fullDescription: The Race Relations Act 1971 prohibits racial discrimination. The Race Relations Commissioner is part of the Human Rights Commission. NZ is increasingly diverse — Asian New Zealanders are now the third largest group after European and Māori. The 2019 Christchurch attacks targeted NZ's Muslim community — a stark reminder of the limits of multiculturalism. AntiAsian racism increased during COVID-19. NZ's bicultural Treaty framework creates tension with multicultural realities.
laws.penalty: Racial discrimination: Human Rights Commission complaints; racial incitement: criminal prosecution up to 3 months
exceptions: Positive measures for disadvantaged groups are not discrimination
Cultural practices and language recognized in some contexts

quiz.q: Which racial or ethnic group has become the third-largest group in New Zealand after European and Māori?
quiz.explanation: Asian New Zealanders have become the third-largest ethnic group in New Zealand (approximately 16% of population) after New Zealand European (70%) and Māori (17%), reflecting NZ's increasing demographic diversity.

laws.title: Corrections Act / Electronic Monitoring
laws.subtitle: Home detention and community sentences
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand's Corrections Act 2004 authorizes electronic monitoring (ankle bracelets) for home detention, parole, and bail conditions. Home detention allows offenders to serve sentences in the community under strict conditions, reducing prison populations. Community service, intensive supervision, and drug testing are also used. The Remand Prisoner (Failure to Appear) Act addresses the high number of remand prisoners (pre-trial detainees) in NZ prisons — about 30% of prison population.
laws.penalty: Breaching home detention or parole conditions: return to prison; new offenses: additional sentences
exceptions: Victims can make submissions about home detention addresses
Electronic monitoring technology has geographic limits

quiz.q: Approximately what percentage of New Zealand's prison population consists of remand (pre-trial) prisoners?
quiz.explanation: Approximately 30% of New Zealand's prison population are remand prisoners — people held before trial awaiting bail decisions or trial outcomes — reflecting both bail decision-making patterns and court backlogs.

laws.title: Freshwater Reforms / Nitrogen Limits
laws.subtitle: Freshwater management and farming impacts
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand's freshwater is significantly polluted by agricultural runoff — nitrogen and phosphorus from dairy farming have degraded rivers, lakes, and aquifers. The Essential Freshwater policy package (2020) set ambitious limits including reducing nitrogen leaching. The reforms generated significant rural opposition. National's 2023 rollback of some freshwater rules was criticized by environmental groups. Te Mana o te Wai (the health of the water) is a Māori concept embedded in water law.
laws.penalty: Freshwater violations: fines; environmental prosecution by regional councils
exceptions: Transitional provisions give farmers time to adjust practices
Critical irrigation infrastructure has modified rules

quiz.q: What Māori concept relating to the health of water has been embedded in New Zealand's freshwater law?
quiz.explanation: Te Mana o te Wai ('the authority of the water') is a Māori concept that has been embedded in New Zealand's freshwater policy framework, recognizing water as having its own health and integrity that must be protected.

laws.title: Waitangi Tribunal / Treaty Settlements
laws.subtitle: Treaty settlements and Crown redress
laws.fullDescription: The Crown has settled over 70 Treaty of Waitangi claims, returning land and paying compensation totaling NZ$2.4 billion+ to Māori tribes (iwi). Settlements are legislated through specific Treaty of Waitangi (Claims Settlement) Acts. Major settlements include Ngāi Tahu (South Island, 1998), Waikato-Tainui (1995), and Ngāpuhi (ongoing). The settlements are 'full and final' in law but many Māori see them as inadequate. Post-settlement governance entities manage returned assets.
laws.penalty: No penalties for Treaty claims; Crown must negotiate in good faith under Waitangi Tribunal jurisdiction
exceptions: Treaty settlements are full and final — no further Crown liability for historical grievances settled
Some claims fall outside Tribunal jurisdiction

quiz.q: Approximately how much has the Crown paid in Treaty of Waitangi claim settlements to date?
quiz.explanation: The Crown has paid over NZ$2.4 billion in Treaty of Waitangi claim settlements to date, across more than 70 settled claims, returning land and providing financial redress for historical grievances against Māori tribes (iwi).

laws.title: Medicines Act 1981 / Medsafe
laws.subtitle: Medicine regulation and Pharmac
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand's medicine regulation involves Medsafe (safety and quality) and Pharmac (government agency that purchases medicines for the public health system). Pharmac's budget-based approach means not all medicines available internationally are funded in NZ — this creates ongoing equity debates, particularly around cancer drugs and rare diseases. Medicines Act governs prescription, pharmacy, and controlled drug rules.
laws.penalty: Unlicensed medicine supply: up to 6 months imprisonment; controlled drug offenses: up to life imprisonment for trafficking
exceptions: Named Patient Supply for unapproved medicines
Compassionate access for experimental treatments

quiz.q: What is the name of the NZ government agency that purchases medicines for the public health system?
quiz.explanation: Pharmac (Pharmaceutical Management Agency) is the NZ government agency that decides which medicines are funded for the public health system, operating within a fixed annual budget to maximize health outcomes.

laws.title: KiwiBuild / First Home Schemes
laws.subtitle: Affordable housing and KiwiBuild failure
laws.fullDescription: The Labour government's KiwiBuild program (2018) aimed to build 100,000 affordable homes in 10 years. It was widely regarded as a policy failure — only about 1,000 homes were built before the target was abandoned. Subsequent housing policies including the First Home Grant, First Home Loan (5% deposit), and Shared Equity schemes have had modest uptake. NZ's housing affordability remains among the worst in the OECD.
laws.penalty: Building Code violations: significant fines; leaky building liability: civil claims
exceptions: Special housing areas have fast-tracked consents
Papakāinga housing (Māori communal) has modified rules

quiz.q: How many homes did KiwiBuild actually build before its 100,000-home target was abandoned?
quiz.explanation: KiwiBuild built approximately 1,000 homes before the Labour government abandoned the 100,000-home target in 2019, making it one of the most high-profile policy failures in recent New Zealand history.

laws.title: Psychoactive Substances Act 2013
laws.subtitle: Legal highs and synthetic drugs
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand's Psychoactive Substances Act 2013 created an unusual framework attempting to allow 'legal highs' (synthetic drugs) to be sold if they passed safety tests. The law required clinical trials on animals, which triggered protests and an amendment banning animal testing — effectively halting the legal market. The Act is widely regarded as a failed experiment. Synthetic cannabinoids remain a significant harm through the illegal market.
laws.penalty: Supply of unapproved psychoactive substances: up to 2 years imprisonment
exceptions: Approved products (none currently approved) could be sold
Low-risk products below defined thresholds

quiz.q: Why did NZ's Psychoactive Substances Act 2013 framework effectively collapse?
options: The Supreme Court struck it down
The products all failed safety tests
Parliament banned the animal testing required for product approval
The EU sanctions threatened NZ trade
quiz.explanation: The Psychoactive Substances Act framework collapsed when Parliament amended it to ban animal testing (responding to public protest), which made it impossible for suppliers to conduct the safety trials needed to get products approved for sale.

laws.title: Afghan and Ukrainian Refugees / Emergency Visas
laws.subtitle: Humanitarian response and emergency visas
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand has responded to humanitarian crises with emergency visa programs — the Afghanistan Emergency Visa (2021, following Taliban takeover) and the Ukraine Visa (2022, following Russian invasion). These supplemented NZ's normal refugee quota. NZ provided special pathways for Afghan interpreters and families with NZ connections. The humanitarian program reflects NZ's foreign policy values and public support for refugee intake.
laws.penalty: Overstaying humanitarian visas: standard immigration enforcement; voluntary return supported
exceptions: Humanitarian visa holders can apply for residence
Emergency extensions available during ongoing conflicts

quiz.q: In which year did NZ create an emergency visa for Afghans following the Taliban takeover?
quiz.explanation: New Zealand created an Afghanistan Emergency Visa in 2021 following the Taliban takeover of Afghanistan in August 2021, providing a pathway for Afghans (particularly those who had worked with NZ forces or NGOs) and their families to come to New Zealand.

laws.title: Māori Land Court / Te Kooti Whenua Māori
laws.subtitle: Māori freehold land and the Māori Land Court
laws.fullDescription: The Māori Land Court (Te Kooti Whenua Māori) is a specialist court managing Māori freehold land — approximately 1.4 million hectares of land in Māori ownership. Māori freehold land has unique rules: it cannot be sold without owner consent, succession passes to descendants, and development requires court approval. Te Ture Whenua Māori Act 1993 governs Māori land. Many urban Māori are disconnected from ancestral land.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized dealing in Māori land: void transactions; civil penalties
exceptions: Papakāinga (communal housing) on Māori land has facilitation

quiz.q: Approximately how many hectares of land are classified as Māori freehold land in New Zealand?
quiz.explanation: Approximately 1.4 million hectares of land in New Zealand is classified as Māori freehold land, governed by Te Ture Whenua Māori Act 1993 and managed through the Māori Land Court (Te Kooti Whenua Māori).

laws.title: Children's Commissioner Act 2003 / Oranga Tamariki
laws.subtitle: Children's rights and CYF reforms
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand's Oranga Tamariki (Ministry for Children) replaced Child, Youth and Family (CYF) in 2017 with a focus on child wellbeing. A 2019 documentary showing the removal of a newborn Māori baby sparked the 'Māori baby uplift' controversy, revealing the disproportionate removal of Māori children from their families. The Independent Review into Oranga Tamariki (2020) found systemic failures. The Children's Commissioner provides independent oversight.
laws.penalty: Child abuse and neglect: criminal prosecution; failure to report: professional sanctions
exceptions: Family Group Conferences preferred over court proceedings
Cultural supports required for Māori children

quiz.q: What controversy in 2019 sparked national debate about the disproportionate removal of Māori children from their families?
options: A report by the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child
A documentary about the removal of a newborn Māori baby
A parliamentary inquiry into Oranga Tamariki
A Waitangi Tribunal report on children's rights
quiz.explanation: A 2019 documentary showing Oranga Tamariki officials attempting to uplift a newborn Māori baby from the hospital sparked national controversy about the disproportionate removal of Māori children from their families by NZ child welfare services.

laws.title: NZX Securities Exchange / Capital Markets
laws.subtitle: NZ Stock Exchange and capital markets
laws.fullDescription: The NZX (New Zealand Stock Exchange) is NZ's primary securities exchange, with approximately 170 listed companies and a market capitalization of ~NZ$150 billion. The Financial Markets Conduct Act 2013 regulates public offers and continuous disclosure. NZ's capital markets are considered relatively small and shallow compared to Australia. The NZX suffered a series of distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) cyberattacks in 2020, highlighting critical infrastructure vulnerabilities.
laws.penalty: Insider trading: up to 5 years imprisonment; misleading disclosure: civil penalties
exceptions: Legitimate hedging transactions exempt from insider trading provisions
Continuous disclosure safe harbors for forward-looking statements

quiz.q: What cyberattack type disrupted New Zealand's stock exchange (NZX) in 2020?
quiz.explanation: The NZX was disrupted by a series of DDoS (Distributed Denial of Service) attacks in August 2020, forcing trading halts over several days in what was one of the most significant cyberattacks on NZ critical infrastructure.

laws.title: COVID-19 Response Act 2020
laws.subtitle: Pandemic response legislation
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand's COVID-19 Public Health Response Act 2020 provided legislative backing for public health orders including lockdowns, border closures, and mandatory isolation. PM Jacinda Ardern's 'go hard and go early' strategy achieved early elimination of COVID-19. NZ went 102 days without community transmission in 2020. The government later transitioned to a vaccination and managed suppression strategy. NZ's strict controls were later relaxed from 2022.
laws.penalty: Breaching COVID orders: fines up to NZ$12,000 for individuals; NZ$15,000 for businesses
exceptions: Essential workers had modified requirements
Compassionate travel exemptions for specific circumstances

quiz.q: How many days without community COVID-19 transmission did New Zealand achieve in 2020?
quiz.explanation: New Zealand went 102 days without community transmission of COVID-19 in 2020, from June to August, demonstrating the effectiveness of its 'go hard and go early' elimination strategy before the Delta and Omicron variants made elimination untenable.

laws.title: Port of Auckland / Logistics Law
laws.subtitle: Ports infrastructure and waterfront disputes
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand's ports are critical infrastructure for an island nation dependent on imports and exports. The Port of Auckland handles about 50% of NZ's imports. The Maritime Union of NZ (MUNZ) has been in prolonged industrial disputes with Ports of Auckland. The government-directed review of NZ's port system recommended rationalization. NZ's geographic isolation means shipping costs and logistics efficiency have significant economic impacts.
laws.penalty: Port safety violations: WorkSafe prosecution; cargo security breaches: Customs Act penalties
exceptions: Trans-Tasman shipping has bilateral arrangements
Coastal shipping has cabotage protections

quiz.q: Approximately what percentage of NZ's imports does the Port of Auckland handle?
quiz.explanation: The Port of Auckland handles approximately 50% of New Zealand's imports, making it the country's most important port for container shipping and a critical piece of economic infrastructure.

laws.title: Child Poverty Reduction Act 2018
laws.subtitle: Child poverty and wellbeing targets
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand's Child Poverty Reduction Act 2018 — a world first — requires governments to set and report on child poverty targets including measures of material hardship and low income. The government must publish annual progress reports against these targets. Child poverty affects approximately 13-17% of NZ children. Māori and Pacific children are disproportionately represented. The cost of living crisis (2022-2023) increased child poverty measures after several years of improvement.
laws.penalty: No criminal penalties; political accountability through annual reporting
exceptions: Measures use multiple indicators to capture different dimensions of poverty
Different time horizons for short-term and persistent poverty

quiz.q: What global first did New Zealand's Child Poverty Reduction Act 2018 achieve?
options: First law to set a child poverty elimination deadline
First law requiring governments to set and report on child poverty reduction targets
First law making child poverty a criminal offense
First law providing universal child income grants
quiz.explanation: New Zealand's Child Poverty Reduction Act 2018 was the world's first legislation requiring governments to formally set and report annually on child poverty reduction targets, embedding accountability for child poverty outcomes into law.

laws.title: Healthy Homes Standards / Rental Quality
laws.subtitle: Minimum rental standards and tenant rights
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand's Healthy Homes Standards (2019), introduced under the Residential Tenancies Amendment Act, require all rental properties to meet minimum standards for heating, insulation, ventilation, moisture/drainage, and draught stopping. The standards phase in compliance deadlines — private landlords by 2024, Kāinga Ora by 2023. Enforcement by Tenancy Tribunal. NZ's rental housing stock is among the worst in the OECD for energy efficiency.
laws.penalty: Non-compliant landlords: Tenancy Tribunal penalties up to NZ$7,200
exceptions: Certain heritage buildings have modified requirements
Short-term rental accommodation (Airbnb) has different rules

quiz.q: What is the name of NZ's minimum rental property standards introduced in 2019?
quiz.explanation: The Healthy Homes Standards, introduced under the Residential Tenancies Amendment Act 2019, require all NZ rental properties to meet minimum standards for heating, insulation, ventilation, moisture control, and draught stopping.

laws.title: Crimes (Intimate Coercion) Amendment 2023
laws.subtitle: Coercive control and intimate partner abuse
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand passed legislation in 2023 specifically criminalizing coercive control in intimate partner relationships — a pattern of behavior designed to dominate and control a partner through psychological manipulation, isolation, monitoring, and threats. Several Australian states had led the way. NZ law now recognizes that serious intimate partner abuse often involves no single obvious violent act but a sustained campaign of control.
laws.penalty: Coercive control offense: up to 5 years imprisonment
exceptions: Single incidents not covered — must demonstrate pattern of behavior
Evidence of pattern gathered through specialist domestic violence investigators
laws.sourceLabel: NZ Ministry of Justice Coercive Control

quiz.q: What type of behavior does NZ's 2023 Crimes Amendment Act specifically criminalize?
options: Coercive control — sustained patterns of psychological control in intimate relationships
quiz.explanation: NZ's 2023 legislation specifically criminalized coercive control — sustained patterns of behavior designed to dominate and control an intimate partner through psychological manipulation, isolation, monitoring, and threats — recognizing abuse beyond physical violence.

laws.title: National Parks Act 1980 / Conservation estate
laws.subtitle: National parks and public conservation land
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand has 14 national parks covering 30%+ of the country's land area, protected under the National Parks Act 1980. The conservation estate managed by DOC includes national parks, reserves, and wildlife sanctuaries. Aoraki/Mount Cook, Fiordland, Tongariro (world's first national park gifted by an indigenous people), and others are UNESCO World Heritage Sites. Tramping (hiking) and ecotourism are significant but also create pressure on fragile ecosystems.
laws.penalty: Damaging national park features: fines up to NZ$100,000; commercial activities without permit: prosecution
exceptions: Traditional Māori cultural practices permitted
Scientific research with DOC permit

quiz.q: What percentage of New Zealand's land area is protected as national parks and conservation estate?
quiz.explanation: New Zealand's 14 national parks and broader conservation estate managed by the Department of Conservation cover over 30% of the country's land area, one of the highest proportions of protected land among OECD countries.

laws.title: Te Kura / Distance Education
laws.subtitle: Correspondence school and remote learning
laws.fullDescription: Te Kura (The Correspondence School) provides distance education for students who cannot attend regular schools — in remote areas, with disabilities, suspended students, and others. NZ has 3-12% of students in alternative education settings. The government funds 20 hours of free early childhood education. NCEA (National Certificate of Educational Achievement) is NZ's secondary school qualification system, periodically reviewed for currency.
laws.penalty: Schools that fail to meet curriculum requirements: ERO (Education Review Office) oversight; Principal and Board sanctions
exceptions: Private schools receive partial government funding with curriculum autonomy
Kura kaupapa Māori (Māori immersion schools) have adapted curriculum

quiz.q: What is NZ's national secondary school qualification called?
quiz.explanation: NCEA (National Certificate of Educational Achievement) is New Zealand's national secondary school qualification, with credits accumulated across Levels 1, 2, and 3 (Years 11-13), offering both subject-based and vocational pathways.

laws.title: Commerce Act 1986 / Market Competition
laws.subtitle: Commerce Commission and market dominance
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand's Commerce Act 1986 prohibits anti-competitive practices including cartel conduct, misuse of market power, and anti-competitive mergers. The Commerce Commission enforces competition law. NZ's small domestic market means many industries are naturally oligopolistic — telecommunications (Spark, Vodafone, 2degrees), retail fuel, banking (the Big Four), and aviation (Air NZ near-monopoly on domestic routes). The Commission has been active in electricity, broadband, and grocery markets.
laws.penalty: Cartel conduct: up to NZ$10 million for companies; individuals up to NZ$500,000
exceptions: Collaborative activities authorized as pro-competitive
Small market-share agreements generally not investigated

quiz.q: How many significant airlines predominantly operate domestic New Zealand air routes?
options: One (Air New Zealand near-monopoly on most routes)
quiz.explanation: Air New Zealand holds a near-monopoly on most domestic New Zealand air routes, with only limited competition from Jetstar on a few routes, making domestic air travel in NZ relatively expensive compared to more competitive markets.

laws.title: Parental Leave and Employment Protection Act 1987
laws.subtitle: Paid parental leave and return to work
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand provides up to 26 weeks of paid parental leave (primary carer) and 1 week for partners, funded by the government at a capped rate (~NZ$712/week). The Parental Leave Act 1987 protects returning parents' job security. NZ's parental leave is more generous than the US (no federal paid leave) but less than Scandinavian countries. The 2022 extension to 26 weeks was a significant step. Working for Families tax credits support low-income parents.
laws.penalty: Denying parental leave: Employment Court remedies; wrongful dismissal after parental leave: compensation
exceptions: Self-employed people have access to paid parental leave
Minimum employment duration required for some leave types

quiz.q: How many weeks of paid parental leave does New Zealand provide to the primary carer?
quiz.explanation: New Zealand provides up to 26 weeks of government-funded paid parental leave for primary carers (from 2020), with 1 week for partners. The payment is capped at approximately NZ$712 per week.

laws.title: Disabled Persons Employment Promotion Act / Enabling Good Lives
laws.subtitle: Employment and disability support
laws.fullDescription: The Enabling Good Lives (EGL) approach, piloted in several NZ regions, gives disabled people greater choice, control, and flexibility over their disability support funding. The Disabled Persons Employment Promotion Act 1960 (now superseded) supported sheltered employment — a model now being transitioned away from toward inclusive employment. The NZ Disability Strategy 2016-2026 sets participation, inclusion, and rights goals.
laws.penalty: Disability discrimination in employment: Employment Relations Authority awards
exceptions: Reasonable accommodation obligations on employers
Supported employment programs provide additional assistance

quiz.q: What approach gives disabled people in NZ greater choice and control over their own disability support funding?
quiz.explanation: The Enabling Good Lives (EGL) approach, piloted in several New Zealand regions from 2012, gives disabled people greater choice, control, and flexibility over their disability support by providing individualized funding they manage themselves.

laws.title: Smokefree Environments Act 1990 / Tobacco Endgame
laws.subtitle: World's strictest tobacco law
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand passed arguably the world's most progressive tobacco legislation with the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Smoked Tobacco) Amendment Act 2022 — a 'tobacco endgame' that would phase out tobacco sales entirely for anyone born after 2008. This would create a 'smoke-free generation'. However, the incoming National government repealed the endgame provisions in 2023, citing concerns about black market stimulation. Anti-vaping measures remain in place.
laws.penalty: Selling tobacco to minors: significant fines; selling tobacco without license: prosecution
exceptions: Vaping products have separate regulation (higher nicotine limits than UK but lower than US)
Export of tobacco products continues under WTO rules

quiz.q: What did NZ's groundbreaking 2022 Smokefree Amendment Act propose for anyone born after 2008?
options: A lifetime ban on purchasing tobacco products
A special tax on tobacco purchases
quiz.explanation: NZ's 2022 Smokefree Endgame legislation proposed that anyone born after 2008 would never be legally able to purchase tobacco products in New Zealand, effectively creating a 'smoke-free generation'. This provision was repealed by the National government in 2023.

laws.title: Digital Services Tax / NZ Tech Economy
laws.subtitle: NZ digital economy and taxation
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand has considered (but not yet implemented) a standalone Digital Services Tax (DST) on multinational tech giants' NZ revenues. NZ instead chose to wait for the OECD's global minimum tax (Pillar 2) and digital tax (Pillar 1) framework. NZ's tech sector includes Xero (cloud accounting), Rocket Lab (space launch vehicles), and a growing startup ecosystem. NZ has one of the highest rates of digital connectivity and digital government services globally.
laws.penalty: Tax evasion by multinationals: Inland Revenue transfer pricing rules; BEPS penalties
exceptions: R&D tax credit available for qualifying technology development
Digital nomad visas allow remote workers to visit NZ

quiz.q: Which NZ-founded company is globally known for cloud accounting software?
quiz.explanation: Xero is a New Zealand-founded cloud accounting software company (founded in Wellington in 2006) that has become one of NZ's most successful tech exports, with millions of subscribers across Australia, UK, and globally.

laws.title: COVID-19 Border Closure / Civil Rights Limits
laws.subtitle: Emergency powers and civil liberties
laws.fullDescription: New Zealand's COVID-19 border closure (March 2020 — July 2022) was one of the world's longest and strictest. NZ citizens and residents were effectively barred from returning home without an MIQ (Managed Isolation and Quarantine) spot — which were allocated by lottery ('the MIQ hunger games'). Legal challenges — including some to the Human Rights Review Tribunal — argued these restrictions infringed fundamental rights to return to one's country.
laws.penalty: Violating border closure: criminal prosecution; MIQ violation: prosecution
exceptions: Emergency travel exemptions for medical and compassionate reasons
Essential workers on critical supply chains exempted

quiz.q: What was NZ's Managed Isolation and Quarantine (MIQ) spot allocation system nicknamed by the public?
quiz.explanation: New Zealand's Managed Isolation and Quarantine (MIQ) spot allocation system was nicknamed 'the MIQ hunger games' by the public, reflecting the competitive and often distressing process of securing a spot to return home during NZ's strict COVID-19 border closure (2020-2022).
